title: AP Psychology: Key Terms

sources.name: Original educational wording based on general subject knowledge

description: For AP Psychology learners: research, brain and behavior, cognition, learning, development, social psychology, and clinical concepts through definitions and examples. For clinical material, verify with current guidelines.

cards.front: What does psychology mean in psychology?
cards.back: The scientific study of behavior and mental processes.
cards.example: A researcher measures how sleep affects attention.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A researcher measures how sleep affects attention.
cards.back: Psychology: The scientific study of behavior and mental processes.
cards.example: A researcher measures how sleep affects attention.

cards.front: What does empiricism mean in psychology?
cards.back: The view that knowledge should be grounded in observation and evidence.
cards.example: A psychologist collects data instead of accepting an intuition as proof.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A psychologist collects data instead of accepting an intuition as proof.
cards.back: Empiricism: The view that knowledge should be grounded in observation and evidence.
cards.example: A psychologist collects data instead of accepting an intuition as proof.

cards.front: What does hypothesis mean in psychology?
cards.back: A specific, testable prediction or proposed explanation.
cards.example: A researcher predicts that spaced practice will improve later recall.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A researcher predicts that spaced practice will improve later recall.
cards.back: Hypothesis: A specific, testable prediction or proposed explanation.
cards.example: A researcher predicts that spaced practice will improve later recall.

cards.front: What does operational definition mean in psychology?
cards.back: A precise description of how a variable is measured or manipulated.
cards.example: Stress is defined in a study as a score on a specified questionnaire.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Stress is defined in a study as a score on a specified questionnaire.
cards.back: Operational definition: A precise description of how a variable is measured or manipulated.
cards.example: Stress is defined in a study as a score on a specified questionnaire.

cards.front: What does replication mean in psychology?
cards.back: Repeating research to see whether a finding occurs again.
cards.example: A second laboratory repeats the same memory experiment with new participants.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A second laboratory repeats the same memory experiment with new participants.
cards.back: Replication: Repeating research to see whether a finding occurs again.
cards.example: A second laboratory repeats the same memory experiment with new participants.

cards.front: What does case study mean in psychology?
cards.back: An intensive investigation of one person or a small number of cases.
cards.example: A researcher closely studies the abilities of one patient after a rare brain injury.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A researcher closely studies the abilities of one patient after a rare brain injury.
cards.back: Case study: An intensive investigation of one person or a small number of cases.
cards.example: A researcher closely studies the abilities of one patient after a rare brain injury.

cards.front: What does naturalistic observation mean in psychology?
cards.back: Recording behavior in an everyday setting without manipulating the situation.
cards.example: An observer records playground interactions without directing the children.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? An observer records playground interactions without directing the children.
cards.back: Naturalistic observation: Recording behavior in an everyday setting without manipulating the situation.
cards.example: An observer records playground interactions without directing the children.

cards.front: What does survey mean in psychology?
cards.back: Collecting self-reported information through questions.
cards.example: Students report their sleep habits in a questionnaire.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Students report their sleep habits in a questionnaire.
cards.back: Survey: Collecting self-reported information through questions.
cards.example: Students report their sleep habits in a questionnaire.

cards.front: What does population mean in psychology?
cards.back: The entire group a researcher wants to understand.
cards.example: All students at a university form the group of interest for a campus study.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? All students at a university form the group of interest for a campus study.
cards.back: Population: The entire group a researcher wants to understand.
cards.example: All students at a university form the group of interest for a campus study.

cards.front: What does random sample mean in psychology?
cards.back: A sample selected through a chance process from a population.
cards.example: Names are randomly drawn from the complete student roster.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Names are randomly drawn from the complete student roster.
cards.back: Random sample: A sample selected through a chance process from a population.
cards.example: Names are randomly drawn from the complete student roster.

cards.front: What does representative sample mean in psychology?
cards.back: A sample whose relevant characteristics reflect those of its population.
cards.example: A campus sample reflects the university's mix of class years and majors.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A campus sample reflects the university's mix of class years and majors.
cards.back: Representative sample: A sample whose relevant characteristics reflect those of its population.
cards.example: A campus sample reflects the university's mix of class years and majors.

cards.front: What does sampling bias mean in psychology?
cards.back: A systematic distortion arising from who is included in a sample.
cards.example: An online-only poll underrepresents people without internet access.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? An online-only poll underrepresents people without internet access.
cards.back: Sampling bias: A systematic distortion arising from who is included in a sample.
cards.example: An online-only poll underrepresents people without internet access.

cards.front: What does correlation mean in psychology?
cards.back: A statistical association between variables.
cards.example: Students who report more sleep also tend to report better concentration.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Students who report more sleep also tend to report better concentration.
cards.back: Correlation: A statistical association between variables.
cards.example: Students who report more sleep also tend to report better concentration.

cards.front: What does correlation coefficient mean in psychology?
cards.back: A number from -1 to +1 describing the direction and strength of a linear association.
cards.example: A value of -0.80 indicates a strong negative linear relationship.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A value of -0.80 indicates a strong negative linear relationship.
cards.back: Correlation coefficient: A number from -1 to +1 describing the direction and strength of a linear association.
cards.example: A value of -0.80 indicates a strong negative linear relationship.

cards.front: What does third-variable problem mean in psychology?
cards.back: The possibility that another factor explains an observed association.
cards.example: Hot weather may explain why both ice-cream sales and swimming increase.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Hot weather may explain why both ice-cream sales and swimming increase.
cards.back: Third-variable problem: The possibility that another factor explains an observed association.
cards.example: Hot weather may explain why both ice-cream sales and swimming increase.

cards.front: What does experiment mean in psychology?
cards.back: A study that manipulates a factor and compares outcomes under controlled conditions.
cards.example: Participants are assigned different practice schedules before taking the same test.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Participants are assigned different practice schedules before taking the same test.
cards.back: Experiment: A study that manipulates a factor and compares outcomes under controlled conditions.
cards.example: Participants are assigned different practice schedules before taking the same test.

cards.front: What does independent variable mean in psychology?
cards.back: The factor manipulated in an experiment.
cards.example: An experimenter assigns either quiet or noisy study conditions.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? An experimenter assigns either quiet or noisy study conditions.
cards.back: Independent variable: The factor manipulated in an experiment.
cards.example: An experimenter assigns either quiet or noisy study conditions.

cards.front: What does dependent variable mean in psychology?
cards.back: The measured outcome in an experiment.
cards.example: The number of words recalled is recorded after each study condition.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? The number of words recalled is recorded after each study condition.
cards.back: Dependent variable: The measured outcome in an experiment.
cards.example: The number of words recalled is recorded after each study condition.

cards.front: What does confounding variable mean in psychology?
cards.back: A factor that varies with the intended manipulation and offers an alternative explanation.
cards.example: The noisy condition is also tested much later in the day.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? The noisy condition is also tested much later in the day.
cards.back: Confounding variable: A factor that varies with the intended manipulation and offers an alternative explanation.
cards.example: The noisy condition is also tested much later in the day.

cards.front: What does random assignment mean in psychology?
cards.back: Placing participants into conditions by chance.
cards.example: A computer randomly assigns volunteers to the treatment or control group.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A computer randomly assigns volunteers to the treatment or control group.
cards.back: Random assignment: Placing participants into conditions by chance.
cards.example: A computer randomly assigns volunteers to the treatment or control group.

cards.front: What does control group mean in psychology?
cards.back: A comparison group used to evaluate the effect of a treatment.
cards.example: One group receives the standard lesson while another receives a new teaching method.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? One group receives the standard lesson while another receives a new teaching method.
cards.back: Control group: A comparison group used to evaluate the effect of a treatment.
cards.example: One group receives the standard lesson while another receives a new teaching method.

cards.front: What does placebo effect mean in psychology?
cards.back: A change associated with expectations about a treatment rather than its specific active ingredient.
cards.example: A person reports relief after receiving an inactive pill believed to be medicine.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A person reports relief after receiving an inactive pill believed to be medicine.
cards.back: Placebo effect: A change associated with expectations about a treatment rather than its specific active ingredient.
cards.example: A person reports relief after receiving an inactive pill believed to be medicine.

cards.front: What does double-blind procedure mean in psychology?
cards.back: A procedure in which participants and relevant investigators do not know treatment assignments.
cards.example: Neither the patient nor the outcome assessor knows which coded pill was given.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Neither the patient nor the outcome assessor knows which coded pill was given.
cards.back: Double-blind procedure: A procedure in which participants and relevant investigators do not know treatment assignments.
cards.example: Neither the patient nor the outcome assessor knows which coded pill was given.

cards.front: What does informed consent mean in psychology?
cards.back: Voluntary agreement after receiving enough information to decide whether to participate.
cards.example: A volunteer reads the study's risks and procedures before agreeing.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A volunteer reads the study's risks and procedures before agreeing.
cards.back: Informed consent: Voluntary agreement after receiving enough information to decide whether to participate.
cards.example: A volunteer reads the study's risks and procedures before agreeing.

cards.front: What does debriefing mean in psychology?
cards.back: Explaining a study after participation, including relevant deception and its purpose.
cards.example: After a deceptive task, researchers explain the true research question.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? After a deceptive task, researchers explain the true research question.
cards.back: Debriefing: Explaining a study after participation, including relevant deception and its purpose.
cards.example: After a deceptive task, researchers explain the true research question.

cards.front: What does mean mean in psychology?
cards.back: The arithmetic average of a set of scores.
cards.example: Scores of 2, 4, and 9 have an average of 5.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Scores of 2, 4, and 9 have an average of 5.
cards.back: Mean: The arithmetic average of a set of scores.
cards.example: Scores of 2, 4, and 9 have an average of 5.

cards.front: What does median mean in psychology?
cards.back: The middle score in ordered data, averaging the middle pair when necessary.
cards.example: For scores of 1, 3, and 20, the central ordered value is 3.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? For scores of 1, 3, and 20, the central ordered value is 3.
cards.back: Median: The middle score in ordered data, averaging the middle pair when necessary.
cards.example: For scores of 1, 3, and 20, the central ordered value is 3.

cards.front: What does standard deviation mean in psychology?
cards.back: A measure of the spread of scores around their mean.
cards.example: Two classes share an average score, but one class has much more dispersed scores.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Two classes share an average score, but one class has much more dispersed scores.
cards.back: Standard deviation: A measure of the spread of scores around their mean.
cards.example: Two classes share an average score, but one class has much more dispersed scores.

cards.front: What does statistical significance mean in psychology?
cards.back: Evidence that results would be sufficiently unlikely under a specified null model and decision threshold.
cards.example: A study's p-value falls below its prespecified 0.05 threshold.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A study's p-value falls below its prespecified 0.05 threshold.
cards.back: Statistical significance: Evidence that results would be sufficiently unlikely under a specified null model and decision threshold.
cards.example: A study's p-value falls below its prespecified 0.05 threshold.

cards.front: What does effect size mean in psychology?
cards.back: A numerical measure of the magnitude of a difference or association.
cards.example: A researcher reports how large the improvement is, beyond whether it is statistically significant.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A researcher reports how large the improvement is, beyond whether it is statistically significant.
cards.back: Effect size: A numerical measure of the magnitude of a difference or association.
cards.example: A researcher reports how large the improvement is, beyond whether it is statistically significant.

cards.front: What does neuron mean in psychology?
cards.back: A specialized cell that receives and transmits information in the nervous system.
cards.example: A sensory cell carries information from the skin toward the spinal cord.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A sensory cell carries information from the skin toward the spinal cord.
cards.back: Neuron: A specialized cell that receives and transmits information in the nervous system.
cards.example: A sensory cell carries information from the skin toward the spinal cord.

cards.front: What does dendrite mean in psychology?
cards.back: A branching neuronal structure that typically receives incoming signals.
cards.example: Inputs from nearby neurons arrive on a cell's branching extensions.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Inputs from nearby neurons arrive on a cell's branching extensions.
cards.back: Dendrite: A branching neuronal structure that typically receives incoming signals.
cards.example: Inputs from nearby neurons arrive on a cell's branching extensions.

cards.front: What does axon mean in psychology?
cards.back: A neuronal projection that carries action potentials toward other cells.
cards.example: An electrical impulse travels away from the cell body along a long fiber.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? An electrical impulse travels away from the cell body along a long fiber.
cards.back: Axon: A neuronal projection that carries action potentials toward other cells.
cards.example: An electrical impulse travels away from the cell body along a long fiber.

cards.front: What does myelin sheath mean in psychology?
cards.back: Insulating material around many axons that supports rapid signal conduction.
cards.example: Insulation around a nerve fiber allows impulses to travel efficiently between gaps.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Insulation around a nerve fiber allows impulses to travel efficiently between gaps.
cards.back: Myelin sheath: Insulating material around many axons that supports rapid signal conduction.
cards.example: Insulation around a nerve fiber allows impulses to travel efficiently between gaps.

cards.front: What does action potential mean in psychology?
cards.back: A brief, propagating change in a neuron's membrane voltage.
cards.example: After threshold is reached, a nerve impulse travels along the axon.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? After threshold is reached, a nerve impulse travels along the axon.
cards.back: Action potential: A brief, propagating change in a neuron's membrane voltage.
cards.example: After threshold is reached, a nerve impulse travels along the axon.

cards.front: What does all-or-none principle mean in psychology?
cards.back: Once threshold is reached, an action potential occurs at full size rather than in proportion to stimulus strength.
cards.example: A stronger stimulus raises firing frequency rather than the size of each spike.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A stronger stimulus raises firing frequency rather than the size of each spike.
cards.back: All-or-none principle: Once threshold is reached, an action potential occurs at full size rather than in proportion to stimulus strength.
cards.example: A stronger stimulus raises firing frequency rather than the size of each spike.

cards.front: What does synapse mean in psychology?
cards.back: The junction where one neuron communicates with another cell.
cards.example: A signal passes from an axon terminal to a neighboring neuron.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A signal passes from an axon terminal to a neighboring neuron.
cards.back: Synapse: The junction where one neuron communicates with another cell.
cards.example: A signal passes from an axon terminal to a neighboring neuron.

cards.front: What does neurotransmitter mean in psychology?
cards.back: A chemical released by neurons to signal across a synapse.
cards.example: Acetylcholine is released at a junction with a skeletal muscle fiber.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Acetylcholine is released at a junction with a skeletal muscle fiber.
cards.back: Neurotransmitter: A chemical released by neurons to signal across a synapse.
cards.example: Acetylcholine is released at a junction with a skeletal muscle fiber.

cards.front: What does reuptake mean in psychology?
cards.back: The transport of released neurotransmitter back into a neuron.
cards.example: A transporter removes serotonin from the synaptic cleft into the presynaptic cell.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A transporter removes serotonin from the synaptic cleft into the presynaptic cell.
cards.back: Reuptake: The transport of released neurotransmitter back into a neuron.
cards.example: A transporter removes serotonin from the synaptic cleft into the presynaptic cell.

cards.front: What does agonist mean in psychology?
cards.back: A substance that activates a receptor and promotes its response.
cards.example: A molecule binds to a receptor and produces a neurotransmitter-like effect.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A molecule binds to a receptor and produces a neurotransmitter-like effect.
cards.back: Agonist: A substance that activates a receptor and promotes its response.
cards.example: A molecule binds to a receptor and produces a neurotransmitter-like effect.

cards.front: What does antagonist mean in psychology?
cards.back: A substance that blocks or reduces receptor activation by an agonist.
cards.example: A drug occupies a receptor without activating it and prevents another molecule from acting.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A drug occupies a receptor without activating it and prevents another molecule from acting.
cards.back: Antagonist: A substance that blocks or reduces receptor activation by an agonist.
cards.example: A drug occupies a receptor without activating it and prevents another molecule from acting.

cards.front: What does central nervous system mean in psychology?
cards.back: The brain and spinal cord.
cards.example: An injury affecting the spinal cord damages this major nervous-system division.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? An injury affecting the spinal cord damages this major nervous-system division.
cards.back: Central nervous system: The brain and spinal cord.
cards.example: An injury affecting the spinal cord damages this major nervous-system division.

cards.front: What does peripheral nervous system mean in psychology?
cards.back: Nerves and ganglia outside the brain and spinal cord.
cards.example: Nerves carrying signals to the fingers belong to this division.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Nerves carrying signals to the fingers belong to this division.
cards.back: Peripheral nervous system: Nerves and ganglia outside the brain and spinal cord.
cards.example: Nerves carrying signals to the fingers belong to this division.

cards.front: What does somatic nervous system mean in psychology?
cards.back: The peripheral system involved in skeletal muscle control and somatic sensation.
cards.example: A person deliberately moves a hand to pick up a cup.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A person deliberately moves a hand to pick up a cup.
cards.back: Somatic nervous system: The peripheral system involved in skeletal muscle control and somatic sensation.
cards.example: A person deliberately moves a hand to pick up a cup.

cards.front: What does autonomic nervous system mean in psychology?
cards.back: The system regulating many involuntary functions of organs and glands.
cards.example: Heart rate and digestive activity change without deliberate commands.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Heart rate and digestive activity change without deliberate commands.
cards.back: Autonomic nervous system: The system regulating many involuntary functions of organs and glands.
cards.example: Heart rate and digestive activity change without deliberate commands.

cards.front: What does sympathetic nervous system mean in psychology?
cards.back: The autonomic division that helps mobilize energy during challenge or arousal.
cards.example: A sudden threat increases heart rate and dilates pupils.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A sudden threat increases heart rate and dilates pupils.
cards.back: Sympathetic nervous system: The autonomic division that helps mobilize energy during challenge or arousal.
cards.example: A sudden threat increases heart rate and dilates pupils.

cards.front: What does parasympathetic nervous system mean in psychology?
cards.back: The autonomic division that supports restorative functions such as digestion.
cards.example: After a threat passes, heart rate slows and digestive activity resumes.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? After a threat passes, heart rate slows and digestive activity resumes.
cards.back: Parasympathetic nervous system: The autonomic division that supports restorative functions such as digestion.
cards.example: After a threat passes, heart rate slows and digestive activity resumes.

cards.front: What does endocrine system mean in psychology?
cards.back: Glands and tissues that release hormones into the bloodstream.
cards.example: The adrenal glands release hormones that affect distant organs.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? The adrenal glands release hormones that affect distant organs.
cards.back: Endocrine system: Glands and tissues that release hormones into the bloodstream.
cards.example: The adrenal glands release hormones that affect distant organs.

cards.front: What does hypothalamus mean in psychology?
cards.back: A brain region involved in homeostasis, motivated behavior, and endocrine regulation.
cards.example: Brain circuits respond to changes in body temperature and thirst.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Brain circuits respond to changes in body temperature and thirst.
cards.back: Hypothalamus: A brain region involved in homeostasis, motivated behavior, and endocrine regulation.
cards.example: Brain circuits respond to changes in body temperature and thirst.

cards.front: What does hippocampus mean in psychology?
cards.back: A medial temporal structure important for forming new declarative memories.
cards.example: A patient has trouble forming new memories of daily events after damage to this structure.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A patient has trouble forming new memories of daily events after damage to this structure.
cards.back: Hippocampus: A medial temporal structure important for forming new declarative memories.
cards.example: A patient has trouble forming new memories of daily events after damage to this structure.

cards.front: What does amygdala mean in psychology?
cards.back: A group of nuclei involved in emotional learning and assessing biologically significant stimuli.
cards.example: A neutral cue gains the ability to evoke fear after pairing with danger.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A neutral cue gains the ability to evoke fear after pairing with danger.
cards.back: Amygdala: A group of nuclei involved in emotional learning and assessing biologically significant stimuli.
cards.example: A neutral cue gains the ability to evoke fear after pairing with danger.

cards.front: What does cerebellum mean in psychology?
cards.back: A brain structure important for coordination, balance, and some forms of learning.
cards.example: A person smoothly adjusts hand movements while learning a motor task.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A person smoothly adjusts hand movements while learning a motor task.
cards.back: Cerebellum: A brain structure important for coordination, balance, and some forms of learning.
cards.example: A person smoothly adjusts hand movements while learning a motor task.

cards.front: What does frontal lobe mean in psychology?
cards.back: A cerebral region involved in planning, voluntary movement, and executive functions.
cards.example: A person evaluates options and inhibits an impulsive response.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A person evaluates options and inhibits an impulsive response.
cards.back: Frontal lobe: A cerebral region involved in planning, voluntary movement, and executive functions.
cards.example: A person evaluates options and inhibits an impulsive response.

cards.front: What does occipital lobe mean in psychology?
cards.back: The cerebral lobe containing primary visual cortex.
cards.example: Damage at the back of the cerebrum disrupts visual processing.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Damage at the back of the cerebrum disrupts visual processing.
cards.back: Occipital lobe: The cerebral lobe containing primary visual cortex.
cards.example: Damage at the back of the cerebrum disrupts visual processing.

cards.front: What does neuroplasticity mean in psychology?
cards.back: The nervous system's capacity to change with experience, development, or injury.
cards.example: Repeated practice alters the strength of connections involved in a skill.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Repeated practice alters the strength of connections involved in a skill.
cards.back: Neuroplasticity: The nervous system's capacity to change with experience, development, or injury.
cards.example: Repeated practice alters the strength of connections involved in a skill.

cards.front: What does sensation mean in psychology?
cards.back: Detection and initial encoding of stimulation by sensory systems.
cards.example: Light stimulates receptor cells in the retina.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Light stimulates receptor cells in the retina.
cards.back: Sensation: Detection and initial encoding of stimulation by sensory systems.
cards.example: Light stimulates receptor cells in the retina.

cards.front: What does perception mean in psychology?
cards.back: Organization and interpretation of sensory information.
cards.example: A viewer recognizes a familiar face from a pattern of light.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A viewer recognizes a familiar face from a pattern of light.
cards.back: Perception: Organization and interpretation of sensory information.
cards.example: A viewer recognizes a familiar face from a pattern of light.

cards.front: What does bottom-up processing mean in psychology?
cards.back: Processing guided initially by incoming sensory features.
cards.example: A reader builds recognition from lines to letters to an unfamiliar word.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A reader builds recognition from lines to letters to an unfamiliar word.
cards.back: Bottom-up processing: Processing guided initially by incoming sensory features.
cards.example: A reader builds recognition from lines to letters to an unfamiliar word.

cards.front: What does top-down processing mean in psychology?
cards.back: Processing influenced by expectations, knowledge, and context.
cards.example: Context helps a reader recognize a partly obscured word.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Context helps a reader recognize a partly obscured word.
cards.back: Top-down processing: Processing influenced by expectations, knowledge, and context.
cards.example: Context helps a reader recognize a partly obscured word.

cards.front: What does absolute threshold mean in psychology?
cards.back: The stimulus intensity detected on a specified proportion of trials, conventionally 50 percent.
cards.example: A faint tone is heard on half of repeated presentations at a certain volume.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A faint tone is heard on half of repeated presentations at a certain volume.
cards.back: Absolute threshold: The stimulus intensity detected on a specified proportion of trials, conventionally 50 percent.
cards.example: A faint tone is heard on half of repeated presentations at a certain volume.

cards.front: What does difference threshold mean in psychology?
cards.back: The smallest difference between stimuli detected at a specified rate.
cards.example: A listener notices a small increase in volume only once it exceeds a certain amount.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A listener notices a small increase in volume only once it exceeds a certain amount.
cards.back: Difference threshold: The smallest difference between stimuli detected at a specified rate.
cards.example: A listener notices a small increase in volume only once it exceeds a certain amount.

cards.front: What does weber's law mean in psychology?
cards.back: The detectable change in a stimulus is approximately a constant proportion of its original intensity over a range.
cards.example: A heavier weight requires a larger added amount before the change is noticeable.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A heavier weight requires a larger added amount before the change is noticeable.
cards.back: Weber's law: The detectable change in a stimulus is approximately a constant proportion of its original intensity over a range.
cards.example: A heavier weight requires a larger added amount before the change is noticeable.

cards.front: What does signal detection theory mean in psychology?
cards.back: A framework separating sensory sensitivity from the decision criterion for reporting a signal.
cards.example: A tired airport screener's accuracy depends on both sensitivity and willingness to flag an item.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A tired airport screener's accuracy depends on both sensitivity and willingness to flag an item.
cards.back: Signal detection theory: A framework separating sensory sensitivity from the decision criterion for reporting a signal.
cards.example: A tired airport screener's accuracy depends on both sensitivity and willingness to flag an item.

cards.front: What does sensory adaptation mean in psychology?
cards.back: Reduced sensory responsiveness during sustained, unchanging stimulation.
cards.example: A room's odor becomes less noticeable after several minutes.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A room's odor becomes less noticeable after several minutes.
cards.back: Sensory adaptation: Reduced sensory responsiveness during sustained, unchanging stimulation.
cards.example: A room's odor becomes less noticeable after several minutes.

cards.front: What does transduction mean in psychology?
cards.back: Conversion of physical stimulus energy into neural signals.
cards.example: Hair cells convert mechanical movement in the inner ear into electrical signals.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Hair cells convert mechanical movement in the inner ear into electrical signals.
cards.back: Transduction: Conversion of physical stimulus energy into neural signals.
cards.example: Hair cells convert mechanical movement in the inner ear into electrical signals.

cards.front: What does rods mean in psychology?
cards.back: Retinal photoreceptors especially sensitive in dim light and not responsible for color discrimination.
cards.example: A person detects a faint object in low light using peripheral vision.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? A person detects a faint object in low light using peripheral vision.
cards.back: Rods: Retinal photoreceptors especially sensitive in dim light and not responsible for color discrimination.
cards.example: A person detects a faint object in low light using peripheral vision.

cards.front: What does cones mean in psychology?
cards.back: Retinal photoreceptors supporting color vision and high acuity under adequate illumination.
cards.example: Bright daylight allows a reader to distinguish fine colored details.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Bright daylight allows a reader to distinguish fine colored details.
cards.back: Cones: Retinal photoreceptors supporting color vision and high acuity under adequate illumination.
cards.example: Bright daylight allows a reader to distinguish fine colored details.

cards.front: What does trichromatic theory mean in psychology?
cards.back: Color vision begins with three classes of cones having different wavelength sensitivities.
cards.example: Different combinations of activity in three cone classes support many perceived hues.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Different combinations of activity in three cone classes support many perceived hues.
cards.back: Trichromatic theory: Color vision begins with three classes of cones having different wavelength sensitivities.
cards.example: Different combinations of activity in three cone classes support many perceived hues.

cards.front: What does opponent-process theory of color mean in psychology?
cards.back: Some color information is coded in opposing channels, such as red-green and blue-yellow.
cards.example: Staring at a colored patch can produce a complementary afterimage.

cards.front: Which psychological concept is illustrated? Staring at a colored patch can produce a complementary afterimage.
cards.back: Opponent-process theory of color: Some color information is coded in opposing channels, such as red-green and blue-yellow.
cards.example: Staring at a colored patch can produce a complementary afterimage.

cards.front: What does binocular disparity mean in psychology?
cards.back: The difference between the two eyes' retinal images, used as a depth cue.

cards.front: What does panic attack mean in psychology?
cards.back: An abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort with rapidly developing physical and cognitive symptoms.
cards.example: Someone suddenly experiences racing heart, trembling, and fear of dying that peaks within minutes.

cards.front: What does obsession mean in psychology?
cards.back: A recurrent, intrusive, unwanted thought, urge, or image that causes distress.
cards.example: A person repeatedly has unwanted contamination thoughts despite trying to dismiss them.

cards.front: What does compulsion mean in psychology?
cards.back: A repetitive behavior or mental act performed according to rigid rules or in response to an obsession.
cards.example: A person repeatedly checks a lock to reduce anxiety even after confirming it is secure.

cards.front: What does major depressive episode mean in psychology?
cards.back: A period of at least two weeks with depressed mood or loss of interest and additional symptoms causing significant distress or impairment.
cards.example: A person has sustained loss of interest, sleep disruption, low energy, and impaired functioning for several weeks.

cards.front: What does mania mean in psychology?
cards.back: A distinct episode of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy and severe functional consequences.
cards.example: A person needs very little sleep, speaks rapidly, and makes risky plans with markedly impaired judgment.

cards.front: What does delusion mean in psychology?
cards.back: A fixed belief that is not readily changed by conflicting evidence and is assessed in cultural context.
cards.example: A person remains convinced of an implausible plot despite strong contrary evidence.

cards.front: What does hallucination mean in psychology?
cards.back: A perception-like experience occurring without the corresponding external stimulus.
cards.example: A person hears a distinct voice when no one is speaking.

cards.back: Reductions in normal functions such as emotional expression, motivation, or speech, often discussed in schizophrenia.

cards.front: What does cognitive behavioral therapy mean in psychology?
cards.back: An approach that works on patterns of thinking and behavior contributing to difficulties.
cards.example: A client tests an unhelpful prediction and practices a new response between sessions.

cards.front: What does exposure therapy mean in psychology?
cards.back: A treatment approach involving planned contact with feared stimuli or situations to change fear learning and avoidance.
cards.example: With a therapist, a client gradually practices entering situations previously avoided because of fear.

cards.back: The consistency of a measurement across relevant repetitions or items.
